# Write Simply

> **Purpose:** `core/pattern-rules.md` says what to cut. This file says what to aim for, and how
> to tell when a draft got there. Loaded on every writing job, right after the pattern rules.
>
> Distilled from three Paul Graham essays: [Write Simply](https://paulgraham.com/simply.html),
> [Good Writing](https://paulgraham.com/goodwriting.html) and
> [Writes and Write-Nots](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html). The observations are his. The rules
> and the vault wiring are mine.

## 1. Simple is the default, complex is a decision

Use ordinary words and short sentences. Keep the technical term and simplify every word around it.

A complicated sentence written on purpose is a tool. A complicated sentence written by accident is
clumsy. Both look the same on the page, so the writer is the only person who can tell them apart.
Never write one by accident.

This rule also protects a draft. An edit that flattens a deliberate long sentence has broken
something, so read the intent before you cut.

## 2. Every sentence spends the reader's energy

A reader arrives with a fixed amount of attention. Energy spent on your prose is energy that never
reaches your idea.

Most readers quit part way through a long piece. Lower friction means more of them finish. That is
the entire return on an hour of cutting.

Fancy writing moves work onto the reader so the writer looks clever. Do not charge them for that.

**What changed in 2026.** The reader now has a model open in the next tab. Ask it your question and
it answers in four sentences, with no warm-up and no history of the field. That is the piece your
draft competes against, and it costs the reader nothing to switch.

So the price of a slow opening moved. It used to cost a little attention. It now costs the whole
reader, because the shorter version already exists and sits one keystroke away. The same holds for
a padded middle and for a term you left unexplained. A reader who has to guess stops guessing and
asks the model instead.

Three faults are fatal now, in this order. The piece takes too long to reach its claim. The piece
buries the claim under qualifiers and clauses. The piece uses a word the reader does not have.
`SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py` checks all three: `slow-lede` for the first, `padded` for the second,
`undefined-term` for the third.

What survives is the part a model cannot produce: the number you measured, the thing you tried that
failed, the decision you made and the reason. Write those first and cut toward them.

## 3. A hard topic does not license hard words

Many readers do not read English first. Their grasp of the idea often runs ahead of their grasp of
the language. Write plainly because the subject is hard. Difficulty never grants permission to stop.

The same choice buys durability. A reader ten years from now sits in the same position as a foreign
reader today, because the language and the references will have moved.

## 4. Plain prose is an honesty test

Complicated writing hides missing ideas, and some writers pick it for that reason. Say nothing
simply and everyone sees it, including you.

So when a sentence resists becoming plain, inspect the idea before you inspect the words. The
resistance is usually the idea, and no rewrite fixes an idea that is not there.

## 5. A sentence that sounds wrong usually means the idea is wrong

Prose that reads well is more likely to be right. The mechanism is simple. You will never rewrite
an awkward passage into a version you believe less, so any forced change moves toward what you
actually meant.

State the claim in the safe direction. Good sound proves internal consistency rather than truth,
because a careful liar also sounds good. Read the signal the other way instead. A passage that
reads badly almost always carries a broken idea inside it.

The diagnostic is one question. When a line reads badly, do not reach for a synonym. Ask what you
meant to say there.

This holds for writing that develops an idea. It does not hold for a piece that reports finished
work, such as a release note or a build report, where the thinking already happened elsewhere.

## 6. Two edits that improve a draft with no new thinking

**Force a length change.** Take one paragraph and make it a line shorter. The constraint is
arbitrary and the result still improves, because a rewrite cannot move away from what you meant.
Use it on any paragraph you cannot fix by argument.

**Read as the first reader.** The writer reads the draft more times than anybody else will. Read it
cold and mark every place where something catches. Then repair the idea at that spot, not the word.

## 7. Rhythm follows the idea, never a meter

Good rhythm is not regular. A simple idea gets a short sentence. A subtle idea needs a long one to
carry its conditions.

An even cadence is therefore a defect, and so is a clipped sentence added for punch. Never
regularise a draft, and never truncate one.

## 8. Writing is thinking, so keep the thinking

Leslie Lamport put the stake plainly: "If you're thinking without writing, you only think you're
thinking."

AI removed most of the pressure to write. The population now splits into writers and non-writers,
which is the same line as the split between thinkers and non-thinkers.

This is the villain in [World](../World.md) wearing a new coat. Handing a draft to a model whole is
renting the thinking. Use a model to draft, to argue and to check. Keep every decision about what
the piece claims.

## 9. The reader was not in the room

Every term has a first appearance. That is the sentence where the reader either
keeps reading or starts guessing.

Guessing costs more than stopping. A reader who stops looks the word up and
comes back right. A reader who guesses reads the next ten paragraphs against
the wrong definition and never finds out.

Two kinds of word cause this, and only one of them is your problem to fix.

**A borrowed term** is real industry vocabulary. `webhook`, `context window`,
`fine-tune`. A reader who searches for one gets the correct answer in a click.
Leave it bare and the reader takes one detour.

**An owned term** is one this vault coined, or bent to a private meaning.
`harness`, `load order`, `state file`, `flywheel`, `second brain`,
`digital twin`, `ICP`. A reader who searches for one of these gets somebody
else's definition and walks away confidently wrong. The internet cannot rescue
that. Only your page can.

So an owned term carries its meaning where it first appears. Four shapes do the
job, and the scorer accepts all four.

| Shape | Example |
|---|---|
| Copula | a harness is everything you build around the model |
| Naming clause | a hook, which is a script that runs on its own |
| Parenthetical | the load order (the sequence those files arrive in) |
| Concepts table | `\| Harness \| Everything around the model \| You own this part \|` |

For a piece that leans on four or more owned terms, put the concepts table
before the argument. Rule 10 in
[Long-Form Writing Rules](../Long-Form%20Writing%20Rules.md) already asks for
this on unfamiliar areas, and it costs the reader twenty seconds.

Numbers break the same rule from the other side. A paragraph carrying four
separate figures hands the reader nothing to hold, so none of them land. Rule 4
of the same file asks for a number per claim. Four numbers in one breath is one
wall, not four claims.

Run the check. `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"`, and CRIT reaches 0.
A hook blocks the write while it does not, because this is the rule a tired
writer skips first.

**Where this came from.** On 2026-09-04 a batch of 49 pieces cleared slop CRIT 0,
LinkedIn format CRIT 0 and SEO 0, and a reader outside the meeting still could
not follow one of them. Every gate measured the words. None of them asked whether
the reader had been handed the words first.

## 10. The pass

Run this with the section 7 checklist in `core/pattern-rules.md`, after the scorer reaches CRIT 0.

- [ ] Read one paragraph aloud. Does any sentence use a word a smart non-native reader would stop on?
- [ ] Find the most complicated sentence in the draft. Was it a decision, or an accident?
- [ ] Find the sentence that reads worst. Fix the idea under it rather than the wording.
- [ ] Take the weakest paragraph and cut it by one line. Keep the shorter version unless it lost a fact.
- [ ] Read the sentence lengths across one section. Is the cadence even enough to feel machine set?
- [ ] Name the decision in this piece that came from you and not from the model. If none exists, stop.
- [ ] List every owned term in the draft. Does each one carry its meaning where it first appears?
- [ ] Find the paragraph with the most figures in it. Can a reader hold all of them?
- [ ] Read the first 40 words alone. Do they carry a figure, a name, a command, or the reader?
- [ ] Ask what a model would answer in four sentences. Does your draft add anything past that?

- [AI Writing Policy](../AI%20Writing%20Policy.md), the top directive

9	# AI Writing Policy
10	
11	> **Purpose:** This is the top rule for any writing that another person will read. Every other
12	> writing file sits under it. [Voice](./Voice.md) says how it sounds. [Long-Form Writing

16	> Adapted from Clay's internal AI writing policy, 2026. The principles are theirs. The wording
17	> and the vault-specific rules are mine.
18	
19	Good writing moves an idea out of one head and into another head, clearly.
20	
21	AI models write fluent text. They do not yet write text you can ship without reading it. As the
22	author, you take the time to confirm that every idea in the piece is an idea you meant to
23	convey. That includes the structure and the emphasis, because the order of the ideas is what
24	decides which ones the reader remembers.
25	
26	Use AI to brainstorm, to draft, and to proofread. Then apply the five principles below.
27	
28	## 1. Stand behind every sentence
29	
30	You own each idea and each sentence in the document before you share it. "The AI wrote that
31	line, ignore it" is not an answer to a reviewer. A reader who finds one sentence you did not
32	mean starts to doubt the other ones. So read the whole thing as if you typed it, because from
33	the reader's side you did.
34	
35	## 2. Writing is thinking
36	
37	The work of deciding what to emphasise is the work of understanding the topic. Skip it and you

type: Identity Profile
title: "AI Writing Policy"
description: "The central directive for every piece of writing an AI helps produce."
created: 2026-08-14
updated: 2026-08-14

# AI Writing Policy

> **Purpose:** This is the top rule for any writing that another person will read. Every other
> writing file sits under it. [Voice](./Voice.md) says how it sounds. [Long-Form Writing
> Rules](./Long-Form%20Writing%20Rules.md) says how it is built. `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py`
> says what is banned. This file says what the writing is for.
>
> Adapted from Clay's internal AI writing policy, 2026. The principles are theirs. The wording
> and the vault-specific rules are mine.

Good writing moves an idea out of one head and into another head, clearly.

AI models write fluent text. They do not yet write text you can ship without reading it. As the
author, you take the time to confirm that every idea in the piece is an idea you meant to
convey. That includes the structure and the emphasis, because the order of the ideas is what
decides which ones the reader remembers.

Use AI to brainstorm, to draft, and to proofread. Then apply the five principles below.

## 1. Stand behind every sentence

You own each idea and each sentence in the document before you share it. "The AI wrote that
line, ignore it" is not an answer to a reviewer. A reader who finds one sentence you did not
mean starts to doubt the other ones. So read the whole thing as if you typed it, because from
the reader's side you did.

## 2. Writing is thinking

The work of deciding what to emphasise is the work of understanding the topic. Skip it and you
finish with a document and no new knowledge. Specs, status updates and retrospectives are
proof of thought, so the artifact is only half the point. Even when AI helps you think, you
understand the problem better after you review the result line by line.

## 3. Spend more time writing than the reader spends reading

A short prompt that becomes a long document moves the cost onto every reader. They can prompt a
model themselves if they want volume. One person paying a one-time cost to cut and sharpen
saves every reader a repeated cost. That trade is always worth it.

## 4. Longer is not better

Length is the easiest thing for a model to add and the hardest thing for a reader to forgive.
A long document hides the real content inside sentences that say nothing. When the piece came
from a short prompt, ask whether the prompt itself is the better artifact.

There is no lossless way to expand natural language. Every rewrite changes the meaning, and the
thing doing the rewrite does not hold your actual intent. Readers want your thoughts, even
rough. Polish that costs information is a bad trade.

## 5. Mark raw AI output as raw

You can quote AI text that fails these standards, as long as you label it. "Claude suggested
this, do you think it is worth a look?" is honest and useful. Passing it off as your own
finished thought is what this policy exists to stop.

## How this gets enforced

1. Read the piece end to end before you send it. No exceptions for short pieces.
2. Run `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` and take CRIT to 0.
3. Cut the document until every paragraph earns its place. Cutting beats adding.
4. When you cannot defend a sentence, delete it rather than rewrite it.

The scorer catches the words. This file catches the reason. A piece can score 0 and still break
this policy, because a clean sentence you did not mean to write is still a sentence you did not
mean to write.

## Related

- [Write Simply](./core/write-simply.md) turns principles 2, 3 and 4 into a working method. It
  carries the plain-style rules, and the test that a sentence which reads badly usually means the
  idea under it is wrong. Always loaded, so it applies to every draft.
- [Runtime contract](./core/runtime-contract.md), the load order (the sequence rule files load in) and the checks.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/write-for-one-reader.md -->
# Write for One Reader and One Claim

Name the one reader before you draft, and decide the one claim they carry away. "Load order decides which rule wins" is a claim. "Load order" is a subject.

## Why

A piece for everyone reads as a piece for no one.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/opening-earns-the-second-sentence.md -->
# The Opening Earns the Second Sentence

Write the first sentence so the reader wants the second one.

## Why

The first sentence is the only one every reader sees.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/each-paragraph-answers-the-last.md -->
# Each Paragraph Answers the Last

Make each paragraph answer a question the paragraph before it raised. Cut or move a paragraph that answers nothing.

## Why

A paragraph that answers nothing is a note, and notes break the thread.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/take-a-position-then-its-limit.md -->
# Take a Position, Then State Its Limit

Take a position, then say where it is weak.

## Why

A claim with no limit reads as marketing. The limit is what a practitioner trusts you for.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/rewrite-by-cutting.md -->
# Rewrite by Cutting, Not Smoothing

Rewrite by cutting and reordering, never by smoothing.

## Why

Smoothing removes the edges that made the draft yours and leaves prose that reads correct and says less.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/read-it-aloud.md -->
# Read It Aloud

Read the draft aloud. Rebuild a sentence you stumble on, because the idea under it is usually wrong.

## Why

The stumble shows the idea is wrong more often than the wording.

The long post that lists a real working setup, step by step, with names and numbers. Atharva bookmarks more of these than anything else, so it earns a slot even though it breaks every rule about brevity.

The best-performing posts in this set almost never open on a hook line. They open on the claim itself. @naval, @nabeelqu, @shl and @karpathy have no hook layer at all, and they are the four sharpest writers in the sample. thanks to the neatlogs team for mentor hours inside a weekend hackathon.

every FirstRun feature passes three tests, or it waits until after #neatHack.

explain: it fits the one-sentence pitch with no second sentence.

score: a judging category needs it.

what the tests cut before kickoff, and what is still cut:

two cuts came back before saturday ended.

a web UI. a share code now replays any run in the browser.
more targets. 6 runs replay on the site, and they opened 4 upstream docs PRs.

the pitch that survived: FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container, finds the first broken step, and proves the fix with a second clean run.

---
type: Tweet
title: FirstRun Pricing Waits for a Measured Cost per Run
source_blog: none
description: "FirstRun's agent could spend $0.50 a run, 30x the mean, and nothing in the business set that number."
created: 2026-10-10
updated: 2026-10-10
posted: false
---

FirstRun's agent could spend $0.50 a run. that is 30x the mean run cost, and nothing in the business set that number.

@neatlogs held 64 traces from saturday. the mean run cost $0.0167 and the p95 run cost $0.0508, at Sonnet list price. at the old cap, one bad month costs a Scale customer 5x their $299 fee.

so the price sets the cap now. @arithecfo built the model on those traces:

cap per run = price / runs a month x (1 - 70% margin floor) - compute

team, $49 for 300 runs: $0.0471
scale, $299 for 3,000 runs: $0.0280
free: $0.0108, the measured median run

on the typer quickstart, the free tier stopped the agent at step 4. it had spent $0.0115 of $0.0108. #neatHack

A8 and A9 are fixed in Zernio, with new text and images and the same slots. A7 is not, because its Zernio post was deleted sometime between 19:52 and 19:56 IST, after I read it and before I updated it. I did not delete it. That points to you or another session.

## What Changed

- **A8, Sun 13:30:** the cut list now holds only what is still cut: the parallel coordinator, the nightly AWS runner and the docs-owner lookup. A new line says two cuts came back on Saturday: the web UI, and the extra targets (6 runs on the site, 4 upstream docs PRs). The image is still the OG card.
- **A9, Sun 16:30:** this is now a cap post with real numbers.
  - The old cap of $0.50 per run was 30x the mean.
  - Across 64 neatlogs traces, the mean run cost $0.0167 and the p95 run cost $0.0508.
  - The formula is `cap = price / runs x (1 - 70%) - compute`.
  - The caps are $0.0108 (Free), $0.0471 (Team) and $0.0280 (Scale).
  - The Free cap stopped a typer run at step 4.
  - The A9 card is rebuilt with these numbers.
- **A7 (tweet file only):** "by 3 PM on saturday it had one", followed by how the share code replays a run. The question for the 1 PM Chetan office hour becomes "where does a judge stop trusting a demo?". The new card holds a real 2x screenshot of the live /run page with step 10 open.

All three files score 0 critical findings on the slop and clarity checks.

## Open Items

1. **A7 needs a decision.** If you deleted it on purpose, I leave it. If not, I reschedule it for Sun 10:30 with the new text and card.
2. **The images are not committed to NOTES.** Zernio keeps an upload for 7 days, which covers Sunday, but the vault is the only lasting copy. The new or changed files are `a7-run-page.*`, `a9-price-waits.*` and `run-page-shot.png` in `META/Attachments/neathack/cards/x/`, plus the two `.jpg` copies in `META/Attachments/neathack/x/`.
3. **The LinkedIn version of A9 has the same stale claim.** It is post `6ac9d3791ae9d196e263f861`, scheduled for Sun 11 Oct 23:00 IST, and it opens "A price built on a guessed cost per run is a guess with a dollar sign." I did not touch it.

content.content:
1	---
2	type: Shot Sheet
3	title: FirstRun demo video shot sheet
4	created: 2026-10-10
5	updated: 2026-10-10
6	---
7	
8	# FirstRun Demo Video Shot Sheet
9	
10	**Hook:** The dbt DuckDB guide never worked in a clean container. FirstRun found the broken step, fixed it, and proved the fix.
11	
12	This sheet plans a 1:55 hero cut from three sources: DJI Action 4 footage, screen captures and motion graphics. It plans the shots only. Nothing here renders a video.
13	
14	Every shot has an ID and a flag. `H` is human footage, `S` is a screen capture, and `M` is a motion graphic.
15	
16	- **Stable** means the shot survives app changes. Shoot it once.
17	- **Re-shoot** means the shot shows FirstRun's own UI or CLI output. Shoot it again if that UI changes.
18	
19	Every number below comes from the README, `hackathon.md`, the landing page or the dbt replay payload in `docs/examples/dbt.txt`. Do not add a number that is not in those files.
20	
21	## The Film Follows One Real Bug for 1:55
22	
23	One story runs the whole film: the dbt guide step `jafgen --years 6`. It breaks, FirstRun fixes it, a clean container proves the fix, and a PR goes upstream. The sponsor tools appear as the reasons each step worked.
24	
25	| Time | Beat | On screen | Optional voiceover |
26	|---|---|---|---|
27	| 0:00 to 0:07 | B1 Cold open | Night desk. A terminal turns red at step 10. | None. Keyboard, then an error thud. |
28	| 0:07 to 0:15 | B2 The problem | Laptop lid closes. Kinetic text. | "Your quickstart is the only part of your product tested by people who leave instead of filing a bug." |
29	| 0:15 to 0:22 | B3 The answer | Wordmark. Enter key in slow motion. | "So I built FirstRun. Give it a docs URL." |
30	| 0:22 to 0:44 | B4 Break | /run stages Read, Plan, Run. Step 10 goes red. | "It plans one step per command. Every step runs in a clean container. Step 10 breaks." |
31	| 0:44 to 1:02 | B5 Fix and prove | The diff. Prove stage at 9/9. The reaction. | "FirstRun calls it a docs bug and patches the step. A second clean container passes 9 of 9." |
32	| 1:02 to 1:12 | B6 When it broke | Bisect timeline, 0.3.1 green, 0.4.6 red. | "jafgen 0.4.6 dropped the flag, 11 months before the guide shipped." |
33	| 1:12 to 1:25 | B7 Pull requests | Four real PR pages. Phone in hand. | "Every verified fix becomes a pull request. FirstRun opened 4 upstream." |
34	| 1:25 to 1:45 | B8 Three tools | neatlogs trace, Entire checkpoint, cfo.ai cash chart. | "neatlogs caught the agent inventing steps. Entire recorded every session. cfo.ai set the agent's budget." |
35	| 1:45 to 1:55 | B9 Close | Share popover, landing page, end card. Morning light. | "Docs that work. Literally. Replay the run at firstrun.atharvashah.com." |
36	
37	The voiceover runs about 110 words, so the music carries the rest. The film also works with no voice, because the on-screen text carries every fact.
38	
39	## Swap a Beat When the App Changes
40	
41	Each beat is one block of shots with its own timing, so a change to the app costs one beat and never the whole film.
42	
43	1. Check the `Flag` column in the shot checklist below.
44	2. Re-shoot only the `Re-shoot` shots inside the changed beat.
45	3. Keep the beat's length. Trim the new take to fit the old slot.
46	4. Rebuild a motion graphic only when a number in it changes.
47	
48	Two changes are likely before Monday. The /run page lives on branch `site/run-overhaul` in `D:\Atharva\firstrun-run` and may not be live yet. A PR may also move from Open to Merged. A merged PR is good news, so re-shoot that page and keep it.
49	
50	## Thirteen Camera Shots Put a Human in the Loop
51	
52	You shoot alone, so every shot below is self-operated. Use the DJI Mimo app on your phone as the remote and the monitor.
53	
54	**Night shots (B1, B2)** sell the problem. Keep the room dark and let the monitor light your face.
55	
56	| ID | Shot | Mount and angle | FOV | Rate | Light | Length | Beat |
57	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
58	| H01 | Wide of you at the desk, room dark, terminal glow | Desk clamp on a shelf, behind and to the right | Wide | 4K 50 | Monitor plus one warm lamp in the background | 3 s | B1 |
59	| H02 | Your face as you read the error, a slow frown | Mini tripod below the monitor edge, low angle | Narrowest | 4K 50 | Monitor as the key light | 2 s | B1 |
60	| H03 | Fingers typing, keys at eye level | Mini tripod on the desk, 15 cm from the keyboard | Narrowest | 4K 100 | Keyboard backlight plus monitor | 2 s | B1, B3 |
61	| H04 | Your hand closes the laptop lid, then the chair rolls back | Low angle, side of the desk | Wide | 4K 50 | Monitor only, so the lid kills the light | 2 s | B2 |

# FirstRun Demo Video Shot Sheet

**Hook:** The dbt DuckDB guide never worked in a clean container. FirstRun found the broken step, fixed it, and proved the fix.

This sheet plans a 1:55 hero cut from three sources: DJI Action 4 footage, screen captures and motion graphics. It plans the shots only. Nothing here renders a video.

Every shot has an ID and a flag. `H` is human footage, `S` is a screen capture, and `M` is a motion graphic.

- **Stable** means the shot survives app changes. Shoot it once.
- **Re-shoot** means the shot shows FirstRun's own UI or CLI output. Shoot it again if that UI changes.

Every number below comes from the README, `hackathon.md`, the landing page or the dbt replay payload in `docs/examples/dbt.txt`. Do not add a number that is not in those files.

## The Film Follows One Real Bug for 1:55

One story runs the whole film: the dbt guide step `jafgen --years 6`. It breaks, FirstRun fixes it, a clean container proves the fix, and a PR goes upstream. The sponsor tools appear as the reasons each step worked.

| Time | Beat | On screen | Optional voiceover |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 to 0:07 | B1 Cold open | Night desk. A terminal turns red at step 10. | None. Keyboard, then an error thud. |
| 0:07 to 0:15 | B2 The problem | Laptop lid closes. Kinetic text. | "Your quickstart is the only part of your product tested by people who leave instead of filing a bug." |
| 0:15 to 0:22 | B3 The answer | Wordmark. Enter key in slow motion. | "So I built FirstRun. Give it a docs URL." |
| 0:22 to 0:44 | B4 Break | /run stages Read, Plan, Run. Step 10 goes red. | "It plans one step per command. Every step runs in a clean container. Step 10 breaks." |
| 0:44 to 1:02 | B5 Fix and prove | The diff. Prove stage at 9/9. The reaction. | "FirstRun calls it a docs bug and patches the step. A second clean container passes 9 of 9." |
| 1:02 to 1:12 | B6 When it broke | Bisect timeline, 0.3.1 green, 0.4.6 red. | "jafgen 0.4.6 dropped the flag, 11 months before the guide shipped." |
| 1:12 to 1:25 | B7 Pull requests | Four real PR pages. Phone in hand. | "Every verified fix becomes a pull request. FirstRun opened 4 upstream." |
| 1:25 to 1:45 | B8 Three tools | neatlogs trace, Entire checkpoint, cfo.ai cash chart. | "neatlogs caught the agent inventing steps. Entire recorded every session. cfo.ai set the agent's budget." |
| 1:45 to 1:55 | B9 Close | Share popover, landing page, end card. Morning light. | "Docs that work. Literally. Replay the run at firstrun.atharvashah.com." |

The voiceover runs about 110 words, so the music carries the rest. The film also works with no voice, because the on-screen text carries every fact.

## Swap a Beat When the App Changes

Each beat is one block of shots with its own timing, so a change to the app costs one beat and never the whole film.

1. Check the `Flag` column in the shot checklist below.
2. Re-shoot only the `Re-shoot` shots inside the changed beat.
3. Keep the beat's length. Trim the new take to fit the old slot.
4. Rebuild a motion graphic only when a number in it changes.

Two changes are likely before Monday. The /run page lives on branch `site/run-overhaul` in `D:\Atharva\firstrun-run` and may not be live yet. A PR may also move from Open to Merged. A merged PR is good news, so re-shoot that page and keep it.

## Thirteen Camera Shots Put a Human in the Loop

You shoot alone, so every shot below is self-operated. Use the DJI Mimo app on your phone as the remote and the monitor.

**Night shots (B1, B2)** sell the problem. Keep the room dark and let the monitor light your face.

**Run shots (B3 to B5)** match the screen captures. Film the real command so the keystrokes match the terminal.

## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. **What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#key=value` state and never the query string — so deep-link to a tab or section with a bare token and keep all other state in the page.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

content.content:
Two detections run on the traces: "docs step broke" and "planner invented a step". The second one flagged 3 planner spans in v1. Investigate traced them to the planner prompt and proposed a stricter one ([evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md](evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md)). A Claude Code session read the detection and its trend over the neatlogs MCP server and applied the fix in commit 3ca6f11. The fix adds code guards that drop invented, placeholder and fake-secret steps.

The integration check read 3 real runs back from persisted traces. See [docs/neatlogs-integration.md](docs/neatlogs-integration.md).
The business plan sets the agent's spending limit. `firstrun econ` reads 64 neatlogs traces and writes [business/drivers.csv](business/drivers.csv) for cfo.ai. The mean run costs $0.0167, and the p95 run costs $0.0508. A 70% margin floor turns those costs into a cap per tier, and `firstrun run --tier scale` stops any run that spends past the cap.

| Tier | Price | Quickstarts | Cap per run | Runs over the cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 1, weekly | $0.0108 | 48.4% |
| Team | $49 a month | 10, nightly | $0.0471 | 7.8% |
| Scale | $299 a month | 100, nightly, with PRs, Bisect and Prerequisite Proof | $0.0280 | 25.0% |

The old fixed cap of $0.50 let one bad month cost a Scale customer's fee five times over. The plan, the Scale fix and every assumption are in [business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md](business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md). The cfo.ai model is public at [https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE). Under the old cap, cash goes negative in month 14.

| Iteration | v1 traces, detections, a fix, v2 traces | The results table below |

## Version 2 Finishes 3 of 4 Quickstarts and Recovers 3 Failed Steps

v1 ran with recovery off. v2 ran after the neatlogs planner fix (3ca6f11), with recovery and verification on. The same four targets ran both times. Cost and duration come from the neatlogs traces in [evidence/before_after_traces.json](evidence/before_after_traces.json). Cost is the Sonnet 5.5 list price and is not billed, because the runs use a subscription token.

| Target | v1 (recovery off) | v2 (neatlogs fix, recovery, verify) |
|---|---|---|
| neatlogs Python SDK | passed 3/3 | passed 3/3 |
| Entire CLI install | failed at step 1, `curl: command not found` | verified 4/4 after 2 fixes, one of them a real docs fix |
| Chroma getting started | passed 3/3 | passed 2/2 |
| OpenAI v0 README (fixture, Wayback 2023-08-02) | failed at step 6, `openai: command not found` | pinned `openai==0.28.1`, then stopped honestly: the example needs an OpenAI key |

| Metric | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Quickstarts that end passed or verified | 2 of 4 | 3 of 4 |
9:## Three Tiers Price by Quickstarts Covered
17:## The Average Run Costs $0.0167, but One in Twenty Costs Three Times That
34:## The Old $0.50 Cap Let a Scale Customer Cost Five Times the Price
45:## The Margin Floor Sets the Cap, and the Agent Enforces It
67:## Scale Needs a Fix, and the Data Names Two
79:## The Planner Fix From the Traces Cut Cost per Run by 24%
88:## cfo.ai Shows the Old Cap Runs Out of Cash in Month 14
103:## Both Scenarios Pay Back Fixed Costs in Month 2
125:## Rebuild the Model From the Traces
Ari built the model in cfo.ai over MCP, in workspace "Atharva CFOAI", page "FirstRun model". Every formula reads its number from a "FirstRun drivers" table, and its "Driver source" column names the neatlogs trace behind each measured cost. The figures below were read back from cfo.ai, not computed by hand. Cost per run is $0.01862, the 64-trace mean plus compute. Gross margin includes Stripe fees.

| Scenario | Scale gross margin | Team gross margin | Month 18 MRR | Month 18 cash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base | 78.3% | 85.1% | $2,069 | $16,832 |
| Growth | 78.3% | 85.1% | $5,427 | $45,220 |
| Tail month: every run at p95 cost | 44.1% | 64.2% | $2,069 | $12,767 |
| Old cap: every Scale run at $0.50 | -406.6% | 85.1% | $2,069 | -$12,131 |
| Scale at $529 | 86.5% | 85.1% | $2,876 (Base plus the $807 Scale gain cfo.ai reported) | $21,293 |
| Scale at 1,500 runs | 87.7% | 85.1% | $2,069 | $17,390 |

Under the old cap, cash first goes negative in December 2027, month 14. Every other Scenario has positive net cash flow, so cfo.ai shows no runway limit. Raising Scale to $529 earns the most cash. Halving the Scale allowance keeps the $299 price and still clears the 70% floor.

## Both Scenarios Pay Back Fixed Costs in Month 2

## Flagship Demo, 1:55
- **Player:** press Play, or the space bar, to watch the whole cut as an animatic. Each frame holds for its planned length, and screen frames slowly push in like the final edit. The side panel shows the voiceover and the sound cue for each shot.
- **Timeline:** five lanes. Beats (B1 to B9), picture (each shot colored by camera, screen or motion), light (night to day), and music cues (beat drop at 0:15, silence before the step 10 error, lift on 9/9, resolve), plus a time scale. Click any bar to jump there.
- **Shot grid:** 35 frames grouped by beat. Filter by Camera, Screen or Motion. Click a frame to load it in the player.
  - **Screen frames** are real captures of the live /run page, the landing page, the 4 GitHub PRs, Entire and cfo.ai, zoomed to what each shot shows.
  - **Camera frames** are sketches of the DJI framing for each H shot: the night desk, the face lit by the monitor, the slow-motion Enter key, the over-the-shoulder shot, the reaction, the phone, the sunrise.
  - **Motion frames** are mockups of the graphics: the error type-on, the kinetic quote, the diff, the 9/9 trio, the bisect timeline, the PR fan, the end card.

## neatlogs and cfo.ai Film, 1:30
This is a 7-row script with 11 frames. It ends on month 14 and the cap per tier. Two orange brackets need your own line on why you like each tool. I did not write those for you.

- **B6 voiceover:** I replaced "11 months before the guide shipped" with the real release date, April 7, 2024. The 11-month figure is in none of the source files.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: write-linkedin-posts
3	description: Write, rewrite and ship LinkedIn posts for Atharva's personal profile as short list posts a stranger can use, in one of six winning templates, then run the checks, the card, the Zernio draft and the in-place Zernio update. Use when asked to write, refine, redo, review, schedule or batch LinkedIn content, fix weak Zernio LinkedIn drafts, or for any LinkedIn post, thought leadership piece or "make this a banger" request.
4	---
5	
6	# LinkedIn Post Writer
7	
8	Every post is a short list that solves one problem for a reader who has never heard of Atharva. Pick one of the six templates in `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Winning Templates 2026.md`, fill it with real facts, and run the checks. Decided 2026-10-09, after Depost's analysis of his last 19 posts.
9	
10	## Pass the Stranger Test Before You Write
11	
12	The reader does not know Atharva, his tools or his projects. Answer these four in writing before the first line.
13	
14	1. **The reader.** Name one job title, such as "a founder shipping a developer tool".
15	2. **The pain.** Write the problem in the reader's words, in one sentence.
16	3. **The takeaway.** Write what the reader does in the next 10 minutes because of this post.
17	4. **The template.** Name it by number and name. Never use the template of the post scheduled just before this one.
18	
19	If the pain only exists inside Atharva's own setup, the post fails. Find the reader's version of the problem, or drop the idea.
20	
21	The insight must be box 4 in `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`: new to the reader, and usable today.
22	
23	## Load These Files First
24	
25	Read `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`, the templates file, then this file. The banned words and punctuation are already in context from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
26	
27	## Follow the Seven Rules in Every Post
28	
29	1. **Open on the reader.** Line 1 names their problem or promises a list they can use. Never open on I, my, we, our, a product name or a tool name. `li_format.py` blocks this as `self-hook`.
30	2. **Make the list the post.** Use 3 to 9 items. Each item is a short name, then a `↳` line that says what it means for the reader. `li_format.py` blocks a post with fewer than 3 items as `no-list`.
31	3. **Explain every name.** A tool, product or term the reader may not know gets one plain line, or it goes. Jev, AgentZ, Magi, harness, vault and digital twin all need one.
32	4. **Keep only useful numbers.** A number stays when the reader can use it or a source is named. A number that only describes Atharva's own setup goes. Never invent a number.
33	5. **Put Atharva in once at most.** One line of proof is enough, such as "I tested this on 40 of my own posts."
34	6. **Keep it short.** The body runs 120 to 260 words. Each paragraph is 1 to 3 short lines.
35	7. **Close with use.** Write a one-line takeaway, then one specific question the reader can answer from their own work. Never "What do you think?"
36	
37	No hashtags. No emoji in the body, except the 🌱 in the follow line. No jargon a reader must search for. No paragraph a reader must read twice.
38	
39	## End Every Post With the Same Three Blocks
40	
41	**1. The comment CTA,** directly above the follow line. One word in caps, and a real resource. Write the whole line in Unicode Mathematical Bold Sans-Serif, never Markdown `**`. The offsets are U+1D5D4 for A to Z, U+1D5EE for a to z, and U+1D7EC for 0 to 9.
42	
43	𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 "𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗖𝗞" 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜'𝗹𝗹 𝗗𝗠 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗽.
44	
45	**2. The follow CTA,** exactly this line:
46	
47	🌱 If you want to stay sharp on Product, AI, Technology, Marketing and content that helps you grow as a builder, click Follow. I publish consistently and keep it practical.
48	
49	**3. The pinned comment,** after a `---` rule:
50	
51	```
52	---
53	### 📌 PINNED COMMENT
54	
55	{2 to 3 sentences of extra value}
56	
57	→ {one URL}
58	```
59	
60	The pinned comment carries one URL and no hashtag. If no URL exists, stop and ask Atharva for one.
61	
62	Only one ask per post. A second plain `Comment "WORD"` line fails as `double-ask`.
63	
64	## Use the Fixed File Shape
65	
66	New posts go in `SOCIALS/LinkedIn/_WIP/<post-slug>/li_<Title>.md`. Check for an existing file on the topic first, and write into it rather than making a second one.
67	
68	```markdown
69	---
70	type: LinkedIn Post
71	title: Caption Title
72	source_blog: "[[Exact Blog Title]]"
73	description: "The hook, one line"
74	created: YYYY-MM-DD
75	updated: YYYY-MM-DD
76	posted: false
77	---
78	
79	[post starts here]
80	```
81	
82	`source_blog` is the article title as a wikilink, or `none`. `media_asset:` and `media_alt:` are added by `groom.py`. Add no other field.
83	
84	## Run the Checks Until Every CRIT Is Zero
85	
86	```bash
87	python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"
88	python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"
89	python SCRIPTS/socials/li_format.py "<file>"
90	python SCRIPTS/pillars/pillars.py "<file>"
91	```
92	
93	Then read the post once as the stranger. If any line needs Atharva's context to make sense, rewrite it.
94	
95	Render the load-order panel with `python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill write-linkedin-posts --file "<path>" --node "<node>" --topic "<idea>" --format "T<n> <template name>" --insight "<box 4 insight>"`.
96	
97	## Ship New Posts as Drafts and Fix Old Posts in Place
98	
99	1. **Card.** Make it with the `social-cards` skill in `META/Attachments/li-images/<slug>/`, then run `python META/Attachments/li-images/_kit/groom.py <slug>`.
100	2. **Commit and push the media first.** Zernio keeps an upload for 7 days, and the repo is the copy that lasts.
101	3. **New post.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_draft.py "<file>"` is the dry run. Add `--live` to save the Zernio draft.
102	4. **Changed post that Zernio already holds.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_update.py "<file>"` is the dry run. Add `--live` to replace the text and the first comment in place. ---
name: write-linkedin-posts
description: Write, rewrite and ship LinkedIn posts for Atharva's personal profile as short list posts a stranger can use, in one of six winning templates, then run the checks, the card, the Zernio draft and the in-place Zernio update. Use when asked to write, refine, redo, review, schedule or batch LinkedIn content, fix weak Zernio LinkedIn drafts, or for any LinkedIn post, thought leadership piece or "make this a banger" request.
---

# LinkedIn Post Writer

Every post is a short list that solves one problem for a reader who has never heard of Atharva. Pick one of the six templates in `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Winning Templates 2026.md`, fill it with real facts, and run the checks. Decided 2026-10-09, after Depost's analysis of his last 19 posts.

## Pass the Stranger Test Before You Write

The reader does not know Atharva, his tools or his projects. Answer these four in writing before the first line.

1. **The reader.** Name one job title, such as "a founder shipping a developer tool".
2. **The pain.** Write the problem in the reader's words, in one sentence.
3. **The takeaway.** Write what the reader does in the next 10 minutes because of this post.
4. **The template.** Name it by number and name. Never use the template of the post scheduled just before this one.

If the pain only exists inside Atharva's own setup, the post fails. Find the reader's version of the problem, or drop the idea.

The insight must be box 4 in `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`: new to the reader, and usable today.

## Load These Files First

Read `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`, the templates file, then this file. The banned words and punctuation are already in context from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

## Follow the Seven Rules in Every Post

1. **Open on the reader.** Line 1 names their problem or promises a list they can use. Never open on I, my, we, our, a product name or a tool name. `li_format.py` blocks this as `self-hook`.
2. **Make the list the post.** Use 3 to 9 items. Each item is a short name, then a `↳` line that says what it means for the reader. `li_format.py` blocks a post with fewer than 3 items as `no-list`.
3. **Explain every name.** A tool, product or term the reader may not know gets one plain line, or it goes. Jev, AgentZ, Magi, harness, vault and digital twin all need one.
4. **Keep only useful numbers.** A number stays when the reader can use it or a source is named. A number that only describes Atharva's own setup goes. Never invent a number.
5. **Put Atharva in once at most.** One line of proof is enough, such as "I tested this on 40 of my own posts."
6. **Keep it short.** The body runs 120 to 260 words. Each paragraph is 1 to 3 short lines.
7. **Close with use.** Write a one-line takeaway, then one specific question the reader can answer from their own work. Never "What do you think?"

No hashtags. No emoji in the body, except the 🌱 in the follow line. No jargon a reader must search for. No paragraph a reader must read twice.

## End Every Post With the Same Three Blocks

**1. The comment CTA,** directly above the follow line. One word in caps, and a real resource. Write the whole line in Unicode Mathematical Bold Sans-Serif, never Markdown `**`. The offsets are U+1D5D4 for A to Z, U+1D5EE for a to z, and U+1D7EC for 0 to 9.

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 "𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗖𝗞" 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜'𝗹𝗹 𝗗𝗠 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗽.

**2. The follow CTA,** exactly this line:

🌱 If you want to stay sharp on Product, AI, Technology, Marketing and content that helps you grow as a builder, click Follow. I publish consistently and keep it practical.

**3. The pinned comment,** after a `---` rule:

```
---
### 📌 PINNED COMMENT

{2 to 3 sentences of extra value}

→ {one URL}
```

The pinned comment carries one URL and no hashtag. If no URL exists, stop and ask Atharva for one.

Only one ask per post. A second plain `Comment "WORD"` line fails as `double-ask`.

## Use the Fixed File Shape

New posts go in `SOCIALS/LinkedIn/_WIP/<post-slug>/li_<Title>.md`. Check for an existing file on the topic first, and write into it rather than making a second one.

```markdown
---
type: LinkedIn Post
title: Caption Title
source_blog: "[[Exact Blog Title]]"
description: "The hook, one line"
created: YYYY-MM-DD
updated: YYYY-MM-DD
posted: false
---

[post starts here]
```

`source_blog` is the article title as a wikilink, or `none`. `media_asset:` and `media_alt:` are added by `groom.py`. Add no other field.

## Run the Checks Until Every CRIT Is Zero

```bash
python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"
python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"
python SCRIPTS/socials/li_format.py "<file>"
python SCRIPTS/pillars/pillars.py "<file>"
```

Then read the post once as the stranger. If any line needs Atharva's context to make sense, rewrite it.

Render the load-order panel with `python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill write-linkedin-posts --file "<path>" --node "<node>" --topic "<idea>" --format "T<n> <template name>" --insight "<box 4 insight>"`.

## Ship New Posts as Drafts and Fix Old Posts in Place

1. **Card.** Make it with the `social-cards` skill in `META/Attachments/li-images/<slug>/`, then run `python META/Attachments/li-images/_kit/groom.py <slug>`.
2. **Commit and push the media first.** Zernio keeps an upload for 7 days, and the repo is the copy that lasts.
3. **New post.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_draft.py "<file>"` is the dry run. Add `--live` to save the Zernio draft.
4. **Changed post that Zernio already holds.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_update.py "<file>"` is the dry run. Add `--live` to replace the text and the first comment in place. It keeps the date, the image and the status, and it refuses a post that is already published. Never delete and recreate a scheduled post.
5. **Schedule.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_schedule.py`. Monday to Friday, 5 posts a week at most, 10:00 AM US Eastern.
6. **Close the session.** Rebuild the desk with `python SCRIPTS/review/build.py`, then commit and push.

`references/pipeline.md` covers the batch review, the patch tool and post day. A batch of 5 or more gets the fresh-agent review in `references/icp-review-brief.md`.

- `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Winning Templates 2026.md`: the six templates, the Depost numbers and the three benchmark posts.

## Template 6, Sort It Into Three Buckets

Use it when the material is a decision rule. Depost wrote the sample below from Atharva's own topics, and it is the model for this template.

```
[The reader's problem in one line.]

[The reframe in one line.]

Sort every [thing] into 3 buckets:

1. [Bucket A]
[One-line definition.]
- [example]
- [example]

2. [Bucket B]
(same shape)

3. [Bucket C]
(same shape)

[Where teams get stuck, in one line.]

[The better path, in one line.]
```

The Depost sample opens "Your AI agent does not need more intelligence. It needs less access." Its three buckets are allowed by default, requires approval, and denied completely.

## Every Template Ends the Same Way
## Write for a Reader Who Has Never Heard of You

The reader is a net new reader. They do not know Atharva, his tools, his vault or his projects. They see one post in a feed and give it two seconds.

So each post passes this test before it ships.

1. Line 1 names the reader's problem, or promises a list they can use. It never opens on "I", "my", "we", "our" or a product name.
2. Every name the reader may not know gets one plain line of explanation, or it goes. Jev, AgentZ, Magi, harness, vault and digital twin all fail without one.
3. A number stays only when the reader can use it or a source is named. A number that only describes Atharva's own setup goes.
4. The list is the post. Use 3 to 9 items. Each item is a short name, then a `↳` line that says what it means for the reader.
5. Atharva appears once at most, as one line of proof: "I tested this on 40 of my own posts."
6. The body runs 120 to 260 words.
7. The close is a one-line takeaway, then one specific question the reader can answer from their own work.

`SCRIPTS/socials/li_format.py` blocks the two checkable parts. A post with no list of 3 items or more fails as `no-list`. A first line that opens on I, my, we or our fails as `self-hook`.

---
type: LinkedIn Post
title: Sort Your Agent Pricing Into Three Buckets
source_blog: none
description: "Your AI agent's spend cap is probably a number nobody chose."
created: 2026-10-10
updated: 2026-10-10
media_asset: "../../../../META/Attachments/li-images/firstrun-neathack-post-4/firstrun-neathack-post-4.jpg"
media_alt: "Three buckets for agent pricing: chosen limits, prices under test at 49 and 299 dollars a month, and measured costs of 0.0167 dollars mean and 0.0508 dollars p95 per run, with the cap derived from the price, and the neatlogs and cfo.ai logos"
posted: false
---

Your AI agent's spend cap is probably a number nobody chose.

FirstRun, my agent that tests docs quickstarts, could spend $0.50 a run. The measured mean was $0.0167, so the cap sat at 30x the real cost.

Sort every number in your agent pricing into 3 buckets:

1. Chosen
Limits you set yourself.
- Free: 1 quickstart a week
- Team: 10 quickstarts a night
- Scale: 100 quickstarts a night, with PRs

2. Under test
Prices you try before you commit.
- Team at $49 a month
- Scale at $299 a month

3. Measured
Numbers only real runs can give you.
- Mean cost per run: $0.0167, from 64 traces
- p95 cost per run: $0.0508
- The spend cap, derived from buckets 2 and 3

Teams get stuck when bucket 3 holds a guess. At the old cap, one bad month costs a $299 customer 5x their fee.

Derive the cap from the price instead.
cap per run = price / runs a month x (1 - margin floor) - compute

@[neatlogs](urn:li:organization:105668039) traced every run and measured the costs. @[cfo.ai](urn:li:organization:106807285) built the plan and set a cap per tier.

Which limit in your agent did nobody calculate?

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 "𝗣𝗥𝗜𝗖𝗘" 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜'𝗹𝗹 𝗗𝗠 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁.
🌱 If you want to stay sharp on Product, AI, Technology, Marketing and content that helps you grow as a builder, click Follow. I publish consistently and keep it practical.

---
### 📌 PINNED COMMENT

With a 70% margin floor, the caps came out at $0.0108 for Free, $0.0471 for Team and $0.0280 for Scale. The free tier then stopped a run at step 4. The full plan names the neatlogs trace behind every cost.

→ https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/blob/main/business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md
